Chapter 4: Challenging the Old Models — The Birth of Behavioral Economics
For years, economics leaned on a simple idea: people always act rationally. The theory was that we carefully weigh our options, run the numbers, and pick whatever brings us the most benefit.
Sounds neat, right? But Kahneman and Tversky saw things differently. Their research uncovered something fascinating—real people don’t always play by these rules. In fact, we often make choices that seem to make no sense at all. Maybe you’ve seen it yourself—someone hangs on to a sinking investment, hoping it’ll bounce back, or refuses to let go when it’s clearly time to cut their losses. Emotions sneak in, and logic sometimes takes a back seat.
What’s wild is that these aren’t just random mistakes. People fall into patterns, and those patterns can actually be studied and predicted.
One of the best examples comes from the world of medicine. Picture this: doctors—folks trained to rely on cold, hard evidence—sometimes show the same biases as everyone else. In one study, doctors faced two treatments for a deadly illness. But here’s the twist: when the options were presented as survival rates, most doctors chose the more aggressive treatment. Switch things up and frame it in terms of mortality rates, and suddenly, their preferences changed.
The takeaway? The way information is framed—whether it’s positive or negative—can totally change how even experts make decisions.
That’s a big deal. If experts can be swayed by how options are presented, what does that mean for things like public policy, law, or business? Kahneman and Tversky believed that if we really want to make smarter choices, we have to understand these mental shortcuts and biases. It’s not just about filling in gaps in knowledge—these errors are baked right into how our minds work.
And these aren’t just one-off mistakes. They’re the result of mental rules we use every day—rules that help us most of the time, but can trip us up in certain situations.
As more people caught on, a whole new field began to grow. Behavioral economics brought together ideas from psychology and economics, aiming to truly understand what drives our decisions.
The message was clear: if we want to design better policies, build smarter products, or just nudge people in the right direction, we need to start with how people actually think and act—not just how we wish they would.
Kahneman and Tversky’s ideas didn’t stay locked in university classrooms. Suddenly, everyone from researchers to business leaders started asking new questions about human nature. Words like “loss aversion”—that feeling where losing something hurts more than gaining feels good—became part of everyday conversations in economics and finance.
Through it all, the heart of their work stayed the same: a deep curiosity about how our minds work, and a belief that if we want to make better choices, we have to start by understanding our own limits.
